study_identification.title: Neurofind: using deep learning to make individualised inferences in brain-based disorders

study_characteristics.study_objective: This study presents Neurofind, a freely available web-based tool that applies normative modeling to structural MRI data to provide individual-level deviation metrics. The tool outputs two main metrics: (1) Outlier Index Score, measuring deviation from normative brain morphology, and (2) Brain Age, predicting age based on brain morphometry. The study demonstrates the tool's application in Alzheimer's disease and schizophrenia.

dataset_name.answer: Human Connectome Project (HCP) Young Adult; HCP Aging; UK Biobank; IXI

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer v6.0; Desikan-Killiany cortical atlas (68 cortical regions); ASEG atlas (33 subcortical structures); total 101 brain regions (ROIs); MRIQC for quality control

quality_checking_detail.answer: MRIQC tool used with 68 image quality metrics (IQMs) including movement, artifacts, and signal-to-noise ratio. Images with probability >0.7 of being unusable were discarded. Outlier detection: participants with at least 10 ROI_rel more than 3 SD away from sample mean were excluded iteratively within each scanner until no additional outliers were identified. Final sample: 3362 participants (from initial 13,918).

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Neuroharmony method used for scanner harmonization. Neuroharmony uses a random forest model to capture the relationship between image quality metrics (IQMs) and ComBat corrections for each brain region. Once trained, Neuroharmony predicts and applies ComBat corrections for unseen scanners based on IQMs extracted from new T1-weighted images. Neuroharmony was trained twice: (1) for Outlier Detection model controlling for age and sex, and (2) for Brain Age model controlling for sex only. Results shown in Supplementary Materials (Figure S1) demonstrate increased p-values from pre- to post-harmonization in Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests across scanner pairs.

modeling_method.answer: Adversarial Autoencoder (AAE) for Outlier Detection; Support Vector Regression (SVR) for Brain Age

response_variable.answer: Volume of 101 cortical and subcortical regions (relative ROI volumes normalized by intracranial volume)

predictor_effects.answer: Age and sex were added as conditioning variables to the AAE such that the model learns a latent representation while accounting for these demographics. For Outlier Detection: age and sex controlled via harmonization. For Brain Age: only sex controlled via harmonization. Scanner effects handled through Neuroharmony harmonization approach (random forest-based ComBat corrections).

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study explicitly addresses multiple nuisance structures. (1) Scanner effects are handled through Neuroharmony harmonization using random forest-based ComBat corrections applied to unseen scanners. (2) Age and sex effects are controlled as conditioning variables in the AAE. (3) Quality control addresses measurement artifacts through MRIQC filtering and iterative outlier detection. (4) The harmonization accounts for site-specific variance by learning relationships between image quality metrics and required corrections. (5) The study validates harmonization efficacy through Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests showing reduced distinguishability between scanner distributions post-harmonization.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Scanner effects on the ROI_rel were mitigated using the Neuroharmony method. Briefly, Neuroharmony uses a random forest model to capture the relationship between IQMs and the corrections for each brain region prescribed by ComBat, a popular harmonisation approach that uses an empirical Bayes framework to correct for additive and multiplicative batch effects. Once this relationship is learned, Neuroharmony predicts and applies the ComBat corrections for a new set of IQMs extracted from an unseen T1-weighted image. [...] To further account for the effect of demographics variables, age and sex were added to the model such that the AAE was conditioned to learn a latent representation whilst taking into account this information. [...] Images with a probability higher than 0.7 were discarded. [...] Since outliers are unexpected in healthy subjects and are likely to be due to artefacts, healthy controls in the train set with at least 10 ROI_rel more than 3 standard deviations away from the sample mean were considered outliers and excluded.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Main text lines 49-51, 108-109; Supplementary Materials section 1.1, Figure S1

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study reports training performance metrics (MAE = 10.5 ± 9.8 years for Brain Age model in train set) and shows distributions of reconstruction errors in the training set (Figure S2), suggesting some form of training data evaluation. However, the paper does not explicitly describe a formal validation strategy using held-out portions of the training data (e.g., cross-validation performance metrics beyond the hyperparameter search). The hyperparameter optimization used 10-fold cross-validation for Brain Age and grid search with 75%/25% train/validation split for AAE, but comprehensive validation metrics across the full training set using these approaches are not fully reported.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: In the train set, the MAE was 10.5 ± 9.8 years. [...] A systematic hyperparameter search for C was conducted using a ten-fold cross-validated grid-search over the search space [...] The number of hidden layers, the number of neurons in each hidden layer, the number of neurons the latent code, batch size and gamma were optimised using grid search in the train set with 75% of the data for training and the remaining 25% for validation of the hyperparameters.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Main text lines 60-61; Supplementary Materials section 1.1

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The paper does not describe validation using an independent held-out healthy control dataset from the same sources (HCP, HCP Aging, UK Biobank, IXI). The clinical datasets (AIBL, MCIC, COBRE) used for exemplar applications include healthy controls, but these are from different domains/cohorts and are used for clinical comparison purposes rather than as independent validation of the normative model on same-domain healthy participants. There is no mention of setting aside a separate test set of healthy controls from the training cohorts for independent validation.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: No explicit text describes independent validation on held-out healthy controls from the same datasets. The clinical exemplar applications state: 'The final data comprised 364 participants in the clinical datasets' including both patients and controls from AIBL, MCIC, and COBRE, but these are used for demonstrating clinical applications rather than validating the normative model itself.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study validates the models on clinical datasets from different domains: AIBL (Alzheimer's disease), MCIC and COBRE (schizophrenia). These datasets are from different sources than the training data and include both patients and healthy controls. The Brain Age model performance on healthy controls from these external datasets shows MAE = 10.0 ± 6.3 years, which is comparable to training performance (10.5 ± 9.8 years), demonstrating generalization. The Outlier Detection model successfully identifies expected patterns in clinical populations, with AD patients showing significantly larger OIS than controls and specific regional deviations matching known pathology.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: Exemplar applications were carried out in three clinical datasets: the Australian Imaging, Biomarkers and Lifestyle Study (AIBL), the MIND Clinical Imaging Consortium (MCIC) and the Center for Biomedical Research Excellence (COBRE) dataset. [...] The overall performance of the brain age model in the healthy controls of the clinical datasets was MAE 10.0 ± 6.3 years. [...] AD patients showed a significantly larger OIS compared to HC [...] AD patients showed significantly larger median OIS for individual ROIs relative to respective HC for bilateral amygdala, hippocampus, inferior temporal gyrus and inferior lateral ventricle.

deviation_metric.answer: Outlier Index Score (OIS): scaled reconstruction error representing number of interquartile ranges away from median in train set. Categories: Within the norm (<0.26), Low (≥0.26), Medium (≥1.1), High (≥2.3) deviations. Brain Age Gap (BAG): difference between predicted brain age and chronological age, normalized according to train set.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Group differences tested using independent-sample t-test or Mann-Whitney U test depending on normality (Shapiro-Wilk test). ROI-level comparisons adjusted using Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Association between OIS/BAG and symptom severity tested with Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) or Spearman's rho (ρ) depending on normality. Symptom measures: MMSE for AD; SANS, SAPS, and PANSS for SZ (normalized across sites and standardized to zero mean unit variance). Heterogeneity quantified using mean pairwise cosine similarity (CS) across ROI-level OIS within predefined brain regions. Statistical significance set at 0.05.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: In AD, 55.2% of patients showed high deviations from normative brain morphology, primarily in temporal-limbic structures and ventricles, with greater homogeneity than controls; SZ patients showed 30.1% with extreme outliers, mainly in hippocampus and pallidum, with greater heterogeneity than controls; both disorders showed signs of accelerated brain aging.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed:
Alzheimer's disease: AD patients (n=61) showed significantly larger overall OIS (Median=2.46, IQR=2.50) compared to HC (Median=0.91, IQR=1.36, p<0.001). Only 3.4% of AD patients had OIS within the norm versus 25.9% of HC, while 55.2% of AD patients versus 13.8% of HC had high deviations. ROI-level analysis revealed significantly larger deviations in bilateral amygdala, hippocampus, inferior temporal gyrus, and inferior lateral ventricle (all p<0.001 after correction). Severity associations: larger deviations in left hippocampus (ρ=-0.28, p<0.05), left amygdala (ρ=-0.28, p<0.05), and left inferior temporal gyrus (ρ=-0.34, p<0.05) correlated with worse MMSE scores. AD patients were more homogeneous (Mean CS=0.54±0.22) than HC (Mean CS=0.31±0.25), particularly in ventricles (CS_AD=0.72±0.20 vs CS_HC=0.56±0.24) and subcortical regions (CS_AD=0.60±0.20 vs CS_HC=0.42±0.20). Brain age: AD patients showed accelerated aging (scaled BAG: M=-0.1±0.4) compared to HC (M=-0.6±0.4, p<0.001).

Schizophrenia: SZ patients (n=134) showed no significant difference in overall OIS (Median=1.38, IQR=1.83) compared to HC (Median=1.10, IQR=1.76, p=0.091). However, 15.8% of SZ patients versus 20.6% of HC had normative brain morphology, with higher proportions in medium/high deviation categories. ROI-level: significant deviations in bilateral hippocampus (left: p<0.01; right: p<0.05) and left putamen (p<0.05) after correction. Severity associations: right hippocampus deviations correlated with both positive (ρ=0.22, p<0.05) and negative symptoms (ρ=0.20, p<0.05). BAG also correlated with positive symptoms (ρ=0.20, p<0.05) but not negative symptoms. SZ patients were more heterogeneous (Mean CS=0.32±0.15) than HC (Mean CS=0.40±0.17), most evident in ventricles (CS_SZ=0.55±0.22 vs CS_HC=0.62±0.23) and subcortical regions (CS_SZ=0.38±0.20 vs CS_HC=0.47±0.21). Brain age: SZ patients showed accelerated aging (scaled BAG: M=0.8±0.5) compared to HC (M=0.6±0.4, p<0.01).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Neurofind is not customizable and designed for general-purpose, transdiagnostic metrics rather than disorder-specific diagnosis or clinical outcome prediction. The Brain Age model does not account for regression to the mean (age bias), requiring age as a covariate in subsequent analyses. Neuroharmony relies on learned associations between image quality metrics and corrections, potentially limiting effectiveness for images with unusual quality metrics. The tool may not be suitable for participants outside the training range (ages 20-80, non-white ethnicities, or MRI field strengths considerably different from 1.5T or 3T). As a research tool, results should not be used for clinical decisions.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: Neurofind is freely available as a web-based platform at www.neurofind.ai, designed for non-expert researchers with minimal technical requirements. The tool automatically performs all preprocessing (FreeSurfer segmentation) and requires only NIfTI format images and basic demographic information. Users can upload single or multiple images in bulk. Processing includes quality control, harmonization, and generation of individualized reports with Brain Age, Outlier Index Score, and regional deviations displayed on glass brain visualizations. The study emphasizes using Neurofind with comparable healthy control groups to control for sample-specific biases. Code for model development is available at https://github.com/MLMH-Lab/neurofind_ai.

general_notes.general_notes: This paper presents a web-based tool (Neurofind) rather than a traditional research study, combining established methods (adversarial autoencoder for outlier detection, SVR for brain age, Neuroharmony for harmonization) into an accessible platform. The exemplar applications serve to demonstrate tool functionality rather than primary research aims. Key technical details: AAE architecture comprises input layer (101 neurons), encoder (1 hidden layer, 25 neurons), latent code (5 neurons), decoder and discriminator (1 hidden layer each, 25 neurons). Training used Adam optimizer with cyclical learning rate (base: 0.00002, max: 0.005). ROI volumes were robustly normalized (median subtraction, IQR scaling) and harmonization was performed separately for each normative model. The study addresses an important gap in accessibility of normative modeling tools, as existing tools focus on neurological disorders (dementia, MS, TBI, epilepsy) with known biomarkers, whereas psychiatric disorders lack such clear markers and exhibit heterogeneous, subtle, widespread abnormalities. Full dataset information: HCP (n=599), HCP Aging (n=458), UK Biobank S01 (n=1462), Biobank S02 (n=349), IXI S01 (n=293), IXI S02 (n=165), IXI S03 (n=36). Clinical datasets: AIBL (n=122 after subsampling), MCIC S01 (n=64), MCIC S02 (n=40), MCIC S03 (n=52), COBRE (n=86). Total 7 scanners in training, 10 scanners including clinical data. The paper provides comprehensive supplementary materials including detailed acquisition parameters, harmonization results, full ROI lists, normality tests, and heterogeneity analyses.
